title: Radha at the edge of the dance
hookLine: spring arrives in the forest, and Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone but her
carry: viraha: longing for god is devotion too

cards: Clove vines curl in a soft southern breeze. Bees hum around the flowering trees. The cuckoo is calling.
Jayadeva piles up the details of spring until the forest seems almost too sweet to stand in. Into it walks Radha, with a friend at her side, and the friend points. Look.

There's Hari, playing in the spring woods, dancing with the young cowherd women. The song's refrain says this season is hard on anyone apart from the one they love. And Radha is standing at the edge of the dance, apart.

teach.h: HARI DANCES IN THE SPRING WOODS.
teach.b: The friend keeps singing, in paraphrase. Here, in the lovely spring, Hari plays, dancing with the young women: a cruel season for those apart from love.
She describes him, one woman after another drawing close, each sure she has his attention.

teach.h: RADHA SLIPS AWAY TO A BOWER.
teach.b: And Radha, the poem says, goes away. Not to confront him. She slips off into a bower of vines, hurt and jealous, and sits by herself.
She doesn't stop loving him. In her song, she remembers him: the flute, the playful glances, the way he looked at her.
Even while she's angry, her mind keeps returning to Hari. She tells her friend that her heart won't let him go, though he's with the others. That's the bhakti the poem cares about.
Devotion, in the Gita Govinda, isn't calm. It has jealousy in it, and hurt, and memory, and the stubborn turning of the heart back to the one it loves.
Some Vaishnava traditions have a name for this longing in separation, viraha, and treat it as a doorway rather than a failure.
Radha's ache at the edge of the dance becomes, for them, a picture of the soul when God seems to be everywhere except close.
For a devotee whose God feels far, that's the teaching: the longing itself is devotion, not failure. The poem doesn't scold her or hurry to fix things.
And somewhere in the forest, as we'll hear tomorrow, Krishna has noticed she's gone.

how: In Vaishnava devotion, the Gita Govinda's songs of Radha's longing are sung and danced, and viraha, longing in separation, is honored as a mood of devotion in its own right.

o: devotion that keeps turning back to God, even in hurt
a vow to stop loving anyone who causes you pain
a calm, pleasant feeling that comes on good days

games.q: spring in the Gita Govinda — tap the pairs.
p: points out Hari in the dance
slips away to a bower of vines

s: when Radha sees Krishna dancing, she stops loving him
she goes off hurt, and her heart keeps returning to him.
the poem describes spring in rich detail before Radha's hurt
clove vines, a southern breeze, bees and the cuckoo.
in Vaishnava devotion, longing in separation is treated as a failure of devotion
viraha is honored as a doorway, not a failure.

games.q: you're Radha. your friend points: Krishna is dancing with the other women in the spring woods. what do you do?
o: walk into the dance and demand his attention.
slip away to a bower, hurt, and keep remembering him.
games.why: Radha goes off to a bower of vines, jealous and hurt, and her song is all about remembering him.

practice: Bring to mind a time you stood at the edge of something, a party, a group, apart from the one you most wanted near, and let the memory be there without arguing, like Radha in the bower.

Notice what the heart does, whether it turns away or keeps turning back. If you pray, you can bring that longing, as it is, to the one you pray to; if not, let spring keep blooming around the feeling.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In Radha's bower, it's viraha: longing that keeps turning back, even when it hurts.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: viraha, separation and the longing it brings, a mood of devotion in Vaishnava traditions.

carryVoice: Your line: viraha, longing for God is devotion too. Tomorrow, Krishna notices she's gone. Day nine hundred seventy-six, done.
